docs.title: Positron
docs.text: A lightweight .NET alternative to Electron. Positron hosts your HTML/JS user interface in the WebView already built into each operating system and gives you a typed C#↔JavaScript IPC bridge, window and app lifecycle, and a project template — with no bundled browser engine.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Positron is a single, RID-agnostic managed .NET assembly. It P/Invokes the system WebView on each platform:

  • macOS — WKWebView (via the Objective-C runtime)
  • Windows — WebView2 (Edge/Chromium, over a Win32 window)
  • Linux — WebKitGTK (via GObject)

Your web content runs in that native WebView; your application logic runs in .NET. A small, validated IPC bridge connects the two — modelled on Electron's contextBridge: a narrow, typed surface, never a raw native handle.

docs.title: Why — the trade-off
docs.text:
Electron ships a full copy of Chromium and Node.js inside every app. That makes bundles large (hundreds of megabytes) and gives each app its own browser engine to keep patched — a real supply-chain and update surface.

Positron takes the opposite bet. It uses the WebView the OS already ships and keeps patched, so a distributable is a few megabytes plus your assets. The cost is deliberate: because each OS has a different engine, you accept minor per-platform rendering differences instead of one identical engine everywhere.

Electron Positron Rendering engine Bundled Chromium (per app) OS-native WebView (shared) App runtime Bundled Node.js .NET (your app) Typical bundle size 100–250 MB+ A few MB + your assets Render consistency Identical everywhere Native per-OS (WebKit / Chromium) Engine patching You ship updates The OS keeps it patched

Project status

Positron is in early development. The IPC core and the macOS backend are implemented and verified end-to-end. The Windows (WebView2) and Linux (WebKitGTK) backends are implemented and compile, but have not yet been exercised on their target platforms.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
using System.Text.Json.Serialization;
using Positron;

var options = new WindowOptions { Title = "Hello", Width = 800, Height = 600 };

App.Run(options, window =>
{
    // JavaScript calls window.positron.invoke("greet", { name }) → this handler runs.
    window.Handle<GreetRequest, GreetResponse>("greet",
        req => new GreetResponse($"Hi, {req.Name}!"));

    window.LoadHtml("<!doctype html><button onclick=\"greet()\">Greet</button>");
}, AppJsonContext.Default.Options); // source-gen context → trim/AOT-safe

internal sealed record GreetRequest(string Name);
internal sealed record GreetResponse(string Message);

[JsonSourceGenerationOptions(PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonKnownNamingPolicy.CamelCase)]
[JsonSerializable(typeof(GreetRequest))]
[JsonSerializable(typeof(GreetResponse))]
internal sealed partial class AppJsonContext : JsonSerializerContext;

// In the web content:
const res = await window.positron.invoke("greet", { name: "world" });
console.log(res.message); // "Hi, world!"

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Positron is MIT-licensed and welcomes issues and pull requests. This page covers developing Positron itself; to build an app with Positron, start at Getting Started.

docs.title: Development setup
docs.text:
• Install the .NET 11 SDK. The repo pins 11.0.100 with latestFeature roll-forward via global.json.

  • Clone the repo and build:

    dotnet build

The solution (Positron.slnx) contains the library (src/Positron), the samples (samples/), the project template (templates/positron-app), and the test projects (tests/Positron.Tests, tests/Positron.IntegrationTests).

docs.title: Validation gates
docs.text:
Run the gates CI enforces before opening a pull request:

dotnet format --verify-no-changes     # style (fix with: dotnet format)
dotnet build -c Release               # must be warning-free — warnings are errors
dotnet test --filter "Category!=E2E"  # unit tests, all platforms

If you touched a native backend, also run the end-to-end check on that platform:

dotnet test --filter "Category=E2E"   # macOS directly; Linux via `xvfb-run`

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Style is defined by .editorconfig and enforced with dotnet format. There is no Prettier (that is a JavaScript tool). Do not reformat code outside the scope of your change.
  • Doc comments are required on public — and non-trivial internal — types and members.
  • Tests accompany new functionality. The IPC core is deliberately testable without a window through the IMessageTransport seam; prefer unit tests there and reserve E2E for the native bridge.
  • Native interop uses source-generated [LibraryImport] and must stay trim/AOT-clean. Platform P/Invoke lives under src/Positron/Backends/<Os>/, guarded with [SupportedOSPlatform].
  • Surgical changes. Keep each PR focused; avoid opportunistic cleanup in unrelated files.

docs.title: Project layout
docs.text: Path Contents src/Positron/ The library — the single managed assembly. src/Positron/Backends/<Os>/ Per-OS WebView backends (Mac, Windows, Linux). src/Positron/Ipc/ IPC router, wire envelope, and the embedded preload bridge. src/Positron/Serving/ app:// static-file resolver. src/Positron/Files/ File-dialog option types. samples/ Runnable example apps (also the E2E targets). templates/positron-app/ The dotnet new positron-app template. tests/ Unit and integration test projects.

docs.title: Platform backends
docs.text: Positron selects a backend at runtime per OS. If you add support or fix a bug on a platform you cannot test locally, say so in the PR so a maintainer on that platform can verify it. See Architecture for how the backends fit together.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide takes you from a clean machine to a running Positron window.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Positron targets .NET 11. Install the .NET 11 SDK for your platform.

Positron P/Invokes the system WebView, so the only extra requirement is that the OS WebView runtime is present:

OS Required runtime macOS None — WKWebView ships with the OS. Windows The WebView2 Evergreen Runtime. It is preinstalled on current Windows; install it if missing. Linux WebKitGTK — install the libwebkit2gtk-4.1 package (e.g. sudo apt install libwebkit2gtk-4.1-0 on Debian/Ubuntu).

Positron ships no native binaries of its own — it calls the libraries the OS already provides.

docs.title: Scaffold a new app
docs.text:
Install the project template once, then create a project from it:

dotnet new install Positron.Templates   # once per machine
dotnet new positron-app -n MyApp
cd MyApp
dotnet run

A window opens showing the bundled wwwroot/index.html, already wired to a C# greet handler over the IPC bridge.

docs.title: The minimal program
docs.text:
A Positron app is a normal .NET console project that calls App.Run. Here is the smallest useful program — a C# handler, a source-generated JSON context, and some content to load:

using System.Text.Json.Serialization;
using Positron;

var options = new WindowOptions
{
    Title = "MyApp",
    Width = 1024,
    Height = 768,
};

App.Run(options, window =>
{
    // JS → C#: window.positron.invoke("greet", { name })
    window.Handle<GreetRequest, GreetResponse>("greet",
        req => new GreetResponse($"Hello, {req.Name}!"));

    window.LoadHtml("""
        <!doctype html>
        <meta charset="utf-8">
        <body>
          <input id="name" value="world">
          <button id="go">Greet</button>
          <p id="out"></p>
          <script>
            document.getElementById("go").onclick = async () => {
              const res = await window.positron.invoke("greet",
                { name: document.getElementById("name").value });
              document.getElementById("out").textContent = res.message;
            };
          </script>
        </body>
        """);
}, AppJsonContext.Default.Options);

/// <summary>Request payload for the <c>greet</c> channel.</summary>
internal sealed record GreetRequest(string Name);

/// <summary>Response payload for the <c>greet</c> channel.</summary>
internal sealed record GreetResponse(string Message);

/// <summary>Source-generated JSON context — keeps the app trim- and NativeAOT-safe.</summary>
[JsonSourceGenerationOptions(PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonKnownNamingPolicy.CamelCase)]
[JsonSerializable(typeof(GreetRequest))]
[JsonSerializable(typeof(GreetResponse))]
internal sealed partial class AppJsonContext : JsonSerializerContext;

docs.title: Why the JSON context is required
docs.text: The third argument to App.Run — serializerOptions — is not optional. Pass a source-generated JsonSerializerContext.Default.Options. This is what keeps a Positron app trim- and NativeAOT-compatible: it exists precisely so an AOT build can never silently fall back to reflection-based serialization and break at runtime. Every IPC payload type (request and response) must be declared [JsonSerializable] on that context.

docs.title: Loading content: inline, file, or a served directory
docs.text:
• window.LoadHtml(string) — load an HTML string directly (shown above).

  • window.LoadUrl(string) — navigate to a file:// or http:// URL. The template uses this to load a bundled wwwroot/index.html:

    string indexPath = Path.Combine(AppContext.BaseDirectory, "wwwroot", "index.html");
window.LoadUrl(new Uri(indexPath).AbsoluteUri);

  • ServeDirectory — for a built SPA (Angular, React, …), set WindowOptions.ServeDirectory and load app://localhost/. This serves the folder over the app:// scheme with a real web origin, correct MIME types, and single-page-application history fallback:

    var options = new WindowOptions { ServeDirectory = "dist" };
App.Run(options, window => window.LoadUrl("app://localhost/"),
    AppJsonContext.Default.Options);

docs.title: App
docs.text:
static class Positron.App

The entry point for a Positron application. App.Run creates the native window and WebView for the host OS, wires the IPC bridge, lets the caller register handlers and load content, then enters the native run loop and blocks until the window closes.

docs.title: App.Run
docs.text:
public static void Run(
    WindowOptions options,
    Action<Window> configure,
    JsonSerializerOptions serializerOptions)

Runs a Positron application. It builds the window, exposes window.positron to the web content, invokes configure with the ready Window, then blocks in the native run loop until the window closes.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Meaning options The window configuration — see WindowOptions. configure Callback invoked with the ready Window before the run loop starts. Register IPC handlers (Window.Handle) and load content (Window.LoadUrl / Window.LoadHtml) here. serializerOptions Required. JSON options for IPC handler argument and result types. Pass a source-generated context's Options property (e.g. MyJsonContext.Default.Options).

All three arguments are validated as non-null and throw ArgumentNullException otherwise.

docs.title: Why serializerOptions is required
docs.text: Passing a source-generated JsonSerializerContext.Default.Options is what keeps a Positron app trim- and NativeAOT-safe — that is the point of Positron's small-footprint model. The parameter is mandatory precisely so an AOT build cannot silently fall back to reflection-based serialization and break at runtime. Declare every IPC payload type [JsonSerializable] on your context. Positron internally combines your resolver with its own built-in-channel context, so the reserved positron.* payloads also serialize correctly under trimming/AOT.

docs.title: Threading
docs.text: App.Run must be called from the process main thread. On macOS AppKit requires it; on Windows the backend establishes an STA message pump on the calling thread. The call does not return until the window closes.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
using System.Text.Json.Serialization;
using Positron;

App.Run(
    new WindowOptions { Title = "MyApp", Width = 1024, Height = 768 },
    window =>
    {
        window.Handle<GreetRequest, GreetResponse>("greet",
            req => new GreetResponse($"Hello, {req.Name}!"));
        window.LoadUrl("app://localhost/");
    },
    AppJsonContext.Default.Options);

internal sealed record GreetRequest(string Name);
internal sealed record GreetResponse(string Message);

[JsonSourceGenerationOptions(PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonKnownNamingPolicy.CamelCase)]
[JsonSerializable(typeof(GreetRequest))]
[JsonSerializable(typeof(GreetResponse))]
internal sealed partial class AppJsonContext : JsonSerializerContext;

docs.title: File Dialogs
docs.text:
namespace Positron.Files

Option types for the native file dialogs shown by Window.ShowOpenFileAsync and Window.ShowSaveFileAsync. All properties on both types are optional — pass null (or omit the options object) to accept OS defaults.

docs.title: OpenFileOptions
docs.text:
sealed class Positron.Files.OpenFileOptions

Options for Window.ShowOpenFileAsync.

Property Type Meaning Title string? Dialog title. Null uses the OS default. AllowedExtensions IReadOnlyList<string>? Allowed file extensions without the leading dot (e.g. ["txt", "md"]). Null or empty allows any file. InitialDirectory string? Initial directory the dialog opens in. Null uses the OS default (usually last-used). 
string? path = await window.ShowOpenFileAsync(new Positron.Files.OpenFileOptions
{
    Title = "Open a document",
    AllowedExtensions = ["txt", "md"],
});

docs.title: SaveFileOptions
docs.text:
sealed class Positron.Files.SaveFileOptions

Options for Window.ShowSaveFileAsync.

Property Type Meaning Title string? Dialog title. Null uses the OS default. SuggestedFileName string? The default file name suggested in the save dialog. AllowedExtensions IReadOnlyList<string>? Allowed file extensions without the leading dot (e.g. ["txt"]). Null or empty allows any extension. InitialDirectory string? Initial directory the dialog opens in. Null uses the OS default. 
string? path = await window.ShowSaveFileAsync(new Positron.Files.SaveFileOptions
{
    SuggestedFileName = "untitled.txt",
    AllowedExtensions = ["txt"],
});

docs.title: From JavaScript
docs.text:
The renderer reaches the same dialogs through the built-in bridge namespaces, which take the same fields (camelCase): positron.dialog.open(options) and positron.dialog.save(options), each resolving to the chosen path or null. See IPC and the file-system tutorial.

const path = await window.positron.dialog.save({
  suggestedFileName: "untitled.txt",
  allowedExtensions: ["txt"],
});

docs.title: WindowOptions
docs.text:
sealed class Positron.WindowOptions

Configuration for the application's main window, supplied as the first argument to App.Run. All properties have defaults; set only what you need.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: Property Type Default Meaning Title string "Positron" The window title shown in the title bar. Width int 1024 Initial content width in logical pixels. Height int 768 Initial content height in logical pixels. Resizable bool true Whether the user can resize the window. Preload string? null Optional extra JavaScript injected at document-start, after the Positron bridge. Null injects only the bridge. ContextMenu ContextMenuMode Default Whether the WebView shows its default (browser) context menu. EnableDevTools bool false Whether to enable the WebView's developer tools (right-click → Inspect, where supported). ServeDirectory string? null When set, serves this directory over the app:// scheme. Null disables serving. ServeEntry string "index.html" The SPA entry document returned for client-side routes under ServeDirectory.

docs.title: Preload
docs.text: Use it to expose an application-specific preload surface. The Positron bridge is always injected first; your preload runs after it, so window.positron is available to it.

docs.title: ContextMenu
docs.text:
public enum ContextMenuMode { Default, Disabled }
  • Default — show the WebView's default context menu.
  • Disabled — suppress it. Common for app-like UIs that provide their own right-click handling in JavaScript. See the context-menu tutorial.

docs.title: EnableDevTools
docs.text: Enable during development; leave off in release builds — see Security.

docs.title: ServeDirectory / ServeEntry
docs.text:
Setting ServeDirectory serves the folder over the app:// scheme with a real web origin, correct MIME types, and single-page-application history fallback (unknown routes resolve to ServeEntry). This is the supported way to host a built SPA such as Angular or React — load it with window.LoadUrl("app://localhost/"). See Architecture for the serving flow.

var options = new WindowOptions
{
    Title = "MyApp",
    ServeDirectory = "dist",   // your built SPA output
    ServeEntry = "index.html", // the default
    ContextMenu = ContextMenuMode.Disabled,
    EnableDevTools = false,
};

docs.title: Window
docs.text:
sealed class Positron.Window

A live Positron window. It wraps the native backend and the IPC router, exposing a small surface for loading content, registering C# handlers callable from JavaScript, pushing events to the web content, and showing native file dialogs. You obtain one via the configure callback of App.Run — you do not construct it yourself.

docs.title: LoadUrl
docs.text:
public void LoadUrl(string url)

Navigates the web content to a URL — e.g. a file:// or http:// address, or app://localhost/ when WindowOptions.ServeDirectory is set. Throws if url is null or empty.

window.LoadUrl(new Uri(Path.Combine(AppContext.BaseDirectory, "wwwroot", "index.html")).AbsoluteUri);

docs.title: LoadHtml
docs.text:
public void LoadHtml(string html)

Loads an HTML string directly into the web content. Throws if html is null.

window.LoadHtml("<!doctype html><h1>Hello</h1>");

docs.title: Handle (synchronous)
docs.text:
public void Handle<TArg, TResult>(string channel, Func<TArg, TResult> handler)

Registers a synchronous C# handler invokable from JavaScript via window.positron.invoke(channel, payload). TArg is deserialized from the invoke payload; the returned TResult is serialized back as the result.

docs.title: Handle (asynchronous)
docs.text:
public void Handle<TArg, TResult>(string channel, Func<TArg, Task<TResult>> handler)

The async overload — the handler returns a Task<TResult>. Use it for I/O-bound work.

window.Handle<GreetRequest, GreetResponse>("greet", req => new GreetResponse($"Hi, {req.Name}!"));

window.Handle<SaveRequest, bool>("save", async req =>
{
    await File.WriteAllTextAsync(req.Path, req.Contents);
    return true;
});

Both TArg and TResult must be declared [JsonSerializable] on the source-generated JSON context passed to App.Run. See IPC and Security (validate handler arguments).

docs.title: Emit
docs.text:
public void Emit<TPayload>(string channel, TPayload payload)

Pushes an event to JavaScript listeners registered via window.positron.on(channel, cb). Fire-and-forget; there is no response.

window.Emit("tick", new Tick(DateTimeOffset.Now.ToString("HH:mm:ss")));

docs.title: Close
docs.text:
public void Close()

Closes the window and exits the native run loop, unblocking App.Run. Raises Closed. Safe to call from a handler or any thread.

docs.title: Closed
docs.text:
public event Action? Closed

Raised after the window's native run loop has been asked to exit via Close. Use it to release app resources (timers, file handles) tied to the window's lifetime.

var timer = new Timer(_ => window.Emit("tick", DateTime.Now), null, 0, 1000);
window.Closed += () => timer.Dispose();

docs.title: ShowOpenFileAsync
docs.text:
public Task<string?> ShowOpenFileAsync(Files.OpenFileOptions? options = null)

Shows a native open-file dialog on the UI thread and returns the selected absolute path, or null if the user cancelled. Read the file with System.IO.File from the host. See OpenFileOptions.

docs.title: ShowSaveFileAsync
docs.text:
public Task<string?> ShowSaveFileAsync(Files.SaveFileOptions? options = null)

Shows a native save-file dialog and returns the chosen absolute path, or null if cancelled. Write the file with System.IO.File from the host. See SaveFileOptions.

string? path = await window.ShowOpenFileAsync(
    new Positron.Files.OpenFileOptions { AllowedExtensions = ["txt", "md"] });
if (path is not null)
{
    string text = await File.ReadAllTextAsync(path);
}

Note

The renderer can reach equivalent functionality through the built-in window.positron.dialog.* / window.positron.fs.* channels — see IPC. These Window methods are the C# host-side API for the same dialogs.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Positron is a single, RID-agnostic managed assembly. There are no bundled native binaries — every platform backend P/Invokes the WebView libraries the operating system already ships. The only types the library exposes publicly are App, Window, WindowOptions (plus ContextMenuMode), and the file-dialog option types. Everything else — the backends, the IPC router, the transport, the serving pipeline — is internal.

docs.title: Component overview
docs.text:
App.Run builds a Window, which owns an IpcRouter. The router talks to an IWebViewBackend — the native backend selected for the host OS. The backend is both the window/WebView host and the IPC message transport.

flowchart TD
    App["App.Run (static entry point)"] --> Window
    Window --> Router["IpcRouter (internal)"]
    Router --> Backend["IWebViewBackend (internal)"]
    Backend --> Mac["MacWebViewBackend<br/>WKWebView · libobjc P/Invoke"]
    Backend --> Win["WindowsWebViewBackend<br/>WebView2 Core · Win32 HWND"]
    Backend --> Linux["LinuxWebViewBackend<br/>WebKitGTK · GObject"]

docs.title: Backend selection
docs.text:
App.Run asks BackendFactory.Create() for a backend. Selection is a runtime OS check — OperatingSystem.IsMacOS(), IsWindows(), IsLinux() — with no bundled engine behind any branch:

OS Backend Native target macOS MacWebViewBackend WKWebView, reached through the Objective-C runtime via libobjc P/Invoke Windows WindowsWebViewBackend WebView2 Core, hosted in a Win32 window (HWND) Linux LinuxWebViewBackend WebKitGTK, reached through GObject

An unsupported OS throws PlatformNotSupportedException. Because the single assembly carries no native payload, there is nothing RID-specific to publish — the managed assembly runs wherever .NET 11 and a system WebView do.

Threading

App.Run must be called from the process main thread. macOS AppKit requires it; on Windows the backend establishes an STA message pump on the calling thread. App.Run blocks in the native run loop until the window closes.

docs.title: Request round trip
docs.text:
An invoke from JavaScript is a sequence-correlated request/response. The preload bridge stamps each call with a monotonic seq, posts it to the native side, and holds a Promise open until the matching result envelope comes back. Events (Window.Emit) are the reverse: a fire-and-forget C#→JS push.

sequenceDiagram
    participant JS as "JS: positron.invoke"
    participant Bridge as "Preload bridge"
    participant Native as "Native message handler"
    participant Router as "IpcRouter"
    participant Handler as "C# handler"

    JS->>Bridge: invoke(channel, payload)
    Bridge->>Native: __positronPostToNative(json)
    Native->>Router: dispatch invoke envelope
    Router->>Handler: deserialize arg, call handler
    Handler-->>Router: result
    Router->>Native: result envelope { ok, payload | error }
    Native->>Bridge: Evaluate(__positronReceive(json))
    Bridge-->>JS: resolve / reject Promise (by seq)

See IPC for the wire envelope and handler registration.

docs.title: Serving a directory over app://
docs.text:
When WindowOptions.ServeDirectory is set, the backend registers a custom app:// scheme. WebView requests to app://localhost/<path> are intercepted by a scheme handler and resolved by StaticFileResolver: it maps the path to a file and MIME type, or — for a client-side (history-API) route it does not recognise — falls back to the SPA entry document (ServeEntry, default index.html). This gives a built SPA a real web origin rather than file:// quirks.

flowchart TD
    Req["WebView requests<br/>app://localhost/x"] --> Scheme["app:// scheme handler"]
    Scheme --> Resolver["StaticFileResolver"]
    Resolver --> File{"File exists?"}
    File -- "Yes" --> Bytes["Return bytes + MIME type"]
    File -- "No (client route)" --> Fallback["Return ServeEntry (index.html)"]
    Bytes --> WV["WebView renders"]
    Fallback --> WV

docs.title: IPC
docs.text: Positron connects C# and JavaScript through a small IPC layer: an internal IpcRouter sitting on top of an IMessageTransport (the native backend). A preload script — injected at document-start on every backend — defines window.positron in the web content. The design mirrors Electron's contextBridge: a narrow, validated surface, never a raw native handle.

docs.title: The wire envelope
docs.text:
Every message crossing the boundary, in both directions, is a single JSON envelope:

{ "kind": "invoke" | "result" | "event", "seq": 1, "channel": "greet", "payload": {}, "ok": true, "error": null }

The kind field is serialized lowercase. Each kind populates only the subset of fields it needs:

kind Direction Fields used invoke JS → C# seq, channel, payload result C# → JS seq, ok, and either payload or error event C# → JS channel, payload
  • invoke is a request/response correlated by seq — a monotonic call id the JS side assigns and the C# side echoes back on the matching result, so the right pending Promise resolves.
  • result carries ok: true with a payload, or ok: false with an error string.
  • event is a fire-and-forget push from C# to JS listeners; it has no seq.

docs.title: C# side: registering handlers
docs.text:
Register handlers on the Window inside the App.Run configure callback. Both synchronous and async handlers are supported:

// Synchronous
window.Handle<GreetRequest, GreetResponse>("greet",
    req => new GreetResponse($"Hello, {req.Name}!"));

// Asynchronous
window.Handle<SaveRequest, bool>("save", async req =>
{
    await File.WriteAllTextAsync(req.Path, req.Contents);
    return true;
});

Argument and result types are (de)serialized using the source-generated JSON context you pass to App.Run. Declare every payload type [JsonSerializable] on that context.

Push an event to the page with Emit:

window.Emit("tick", new Tick(DateTimeOffset.Now.ToString("HH:mm:ss")));

docs.title: JavaScript side: window.positron
docs.text: The preload bridge installs a frozen window.positron object (it never double-installs, and is not writable or reconfigurable):

docs.title: invoke(channel, payload) → Promise
docs.text:
Calls a C# channel handler and resolves with its result. Rejects if the handler throws or the channel is invalid.

const res = await window.positron.invoke("greet", { name: "world" });
console.log(res.message);

docs.title: on(channel, cb) → () => void
docs.text:
Subscribes to events pushed from C# on a channel. Returns an unsubscribe function.

const off = window.positron.on("tick", (payload) => console.log("tick", payload.time));
// later:
off();

docs.title: Built-in namespaces
docs.text:
The host registers reserved positron.* channels so apps get file dialogs and text-file I/O without writing their own handlers. The bridge exposes them as convenience namespaces over invoke:

JS call Resolves to positron.dialog.open(options) the chosen path, or null if cancelled positron.dialog.save(options) the chosen path, or null if cancelled positron.fs.readText(path) the file's UTF-8 contents positron.fs.writeText(path, contents) completes when written 
const path = await window.positron.dialog.open({ allowedExtensions: ["txt", "md"] });
if (path) {
  const text = await window.positron.fs.readText(path);
}

Dialog options mirror the C# file-dialog option types: title, allowedExtensions (no leading dot), initialDirectory, and — for save — suggestedFileName.

docs.title: How the seams connect
docs.text:
The bridge is backend-agnostic. The native host wires two seams around the injected script:

  • window.__positronPostToNative(json) — set by the backend; sends a JS → C# message.
  • window.__positronReceive(json) — defined by the bridge; the backend calls it to deliver a C# → JS result or event.

A faulty event listener is isolated — one throwing callback does not break delivery to the others. See Architecture for the full round-trip sequence.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Positron's security model follows the same principle as Electron's contextBridge: the web content never touches a native handle. It gets a small, frozen, validated JavaScript surface (window.positron), and everything privileged happens in C#, behind a boundary you control.

docs.title: The isolation boundary
docs.text: The preload bridge exposes window.positron as a frozen object — not writable, not reconfigurable, installed once and never replaced. Page script can call invoke and on; it cannot reach into the transport, swap the bridge, or obtain a reference to any OS object. The only way across the boundary is a channel you registered in C#.

docs.title: Validate handler arguments
docs.text:
A handler's argument arrives as JSON deserialized from the renderer — it is untrusted input from the system boundary. Validate it the same way you would validate any external request:

window.Handle<ReadRequest, string>("readConfig", req =>
{
    // The renderer chose this path. Do not trust it blindly.
    string full = Path.GetFullPath(req.Path);
    if (!full.StartsWith(_allowedRoot, StringComparison.Ordinal))
        throw new InvalidOperationException("Path outside allowed root.");

    return File.ReadAllText(full);
});

The host decides what each channel is allowed to do. A handler is the right place to enforce path allow-lists, size limits, and argument shape — there is no implicit privilege granted to the renderer.

docs.title: Errors stay host-side
docs.text: When a handler throws, the renderer receives a generic failure — the result envelope carries ok: false with a plain error message, and the JS Promise rejects with an Error. Internal specifics (stack traces, file-system layout, secrets in exception text) are not marshalled to the page. Keep diagnostic detail in host-side logging; the renderer only learns that the call failed.

docs.title: File access is mediated
docs.text: The WebView never gets raw file-system access. The built-in positron.fs.readText / positron.fs.writeText channels and the native file dialogs run in C#, on the host. The renderer can only ask; the host performs the I/O and can refuse, sandbox, or audit it. If you need stricter control than the built-ins provide, register your own channels and omit or wrap the built-in behaviour.

docs.title: Content Security Policy
docs.text:
Positron does not impose a CSP for you — set one in your page's <head> to constrain what the rendered content may load and execute:

<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"
      content="default-src 'self' app:; script-src 'self'; object-src 'none'">

A restrictive CSP is the renderer-side complement to the C# boundary: the boundary controls what native capabilities the page can reach, and the CSP controls what the page itself is allowed to load and run.

docs.title: Development vs. release
docs.text: WindowOptions.EnableDevTools defaults to false. Enable it during development for the WebView's inspector; leave it off in release builds.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Treat every handler argument as untrusted; validate at the boundary.
  • Enforce path allow-lists before touching the file system.
  • Let handler exceptions surface as generic failures — never leak internals to the renderer.
  • Set a restrictive CSP in the page <head>.
  • Expose the smallest set of channels your UI actually needs.
  • Disable dev tools in release builds.

docs.title: Packaging
docs.text:
Positron apps are ordinary dotnet publish output: a windowed native executable that P/Invokes the operating system's WebView (WKWebView on macOS, WebView2 on Windows, WebKitGTK on Linux). There is no bundled browser engine, so packaging is mostly about (1) producing a self-contained publish for the target OS and (2) wrapping it in the native installable format users expect, while ensuring the OS WebView runtime is available.

This section documents the scripts under scripts/packaging/ and the tradeoffs behind each platform's approach.

Platform Script Produces Guide macOS macos-bundle.sh + Info.plist.template + entitlements.plist universal .app (optionally signed/notarized) macOS Linux flatpak-build.sh + flatpak/ manifest set .flatpak single-file bundle Linux Windows windows-publish.ps1 self-contained folder + .zip Windows

All scripts take an example app name of PositronApp (the name produced by dotnet new positron-app) with variables at the top you can override for your own app.

docs.title: The example app name
docs.text:
The dotnet new positron-app template creates PositronApp.csproj, so the published apphost binary is named PositronApp. Every script defaults APP_NAME=PositronApp and derives the apphost filename, bundle id, launcher name, etc. from it. Override APP_NAME (and PROJECT, BUNDLE_ID, VERSION) to package your own app — for example to package the repository sample whose assembly name is Positron.Sample.Hello:

APP_NAME=Positron.Sample.Hello \
PROJECT=samples/Positron.Sample.Hello/Positron.Sample.Hello.csproj \
scripts/packaging/macos-bundle.sh

docs.title: NativeAOT and why it matters for packaging
docs.text:
Positron's interop is [LibraryImport] source-generated and its JSON uses source generation, so the library is trim- and NativeAOT-ready. Publishing with NativeAOT (PublishAot=true) produces a single lean native binary with no JIT and no runtime code generation. That has a direct packaging benefit on macOS: because nothing JITs, the hardened-runtime entitlements can stay minimal — you can omit com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit and the unsigned-executable-memory entitlement entirely (see macOS and scripts/packaging/entitlements.plist). A smaller entitlement set is a smaller attack surface and a smoother notarization.

NativeAOT cross-compilation has toolchain prerequisites (a native toolchain for each target), so the macOS script exposes POSITRON_AOT (default on) which you can set to 0 to fall back to a plain self-contained CoreCLR publish — at the cost of needing the JIT entitlement.

docs.title: WebView runtime per platform (summary)
docs.text:
OS Runtime Bundled? macOS WebKit.framework (WKWebView) No — ships with macOS. Nothing to bundle. Windows WebView2 Evergreen Runtime No — preinstalled on Windows 11; detect + offer bootstrapper on older Windows. The native WebView2Loader.dll must ship next to the exe. Linux libwebkit2gtk-4.1 No — provided by the GNOME Flatpak runtime (org.gnome.Platform//49).

See each platform guide for the details and the authoritative vendor documentation.

docs.title: Packaging for Linux
docs.text:
Produces a Flatpak single-file bundle (PositronApp.flatpak).

Script: scripts/packaging/flatpak-build.sh Manifest set: scripts/packaging/flatpak/ — io.github.positron.PositronApp.yaml (manifest), .desktop, .metainfo.xml, .svg icon.

Note: the Flatpak build steps are untested on macOS — flatpak and flatpak-builder are Linux-only. Run flatpak-build.sh on a Linux host or CI runner. The dotnet publish step works anywhere; only the flatpak commands require Linux.

docs.title: Why Flatpak, and why the GNOME runtime
docs.text:
Positron renders through libwebkit2gtk-4.1 (WebKitGTK). The critical packaging fact: that library ships in the GNOME Flatpak runtime (org.gnome.Platform), not the freedesktop runtime. So the manifest bases on:

runtime: org.gnome.Platform
runtime-version: '49'
sdk: org.gnome.Sdk

Version 49 is the GNOME runtime series that carries libwebkit2gtk-4.1. Because the runtime provides WebKit, the app bundles no WebView engine of its own — consistent with Positron's whole premise. If you based on org.freedesktop.Platform you would have to build and bundle WebKitGTK yourself, which defeats the point.

docs.title: How the manifest is structured
docs.text:
buildsystem: simple — we do not compile inside flatpak-builder. Instead:

  1. flatpak-build.sh runs dotnet publish -r linux-x64 --self-contained into scripts/packaging/flatpak/publish/.
  2. The manifest consumes that directory as a local dir source and its build-commands:
  3. copy the payload into /app/positron/,
  4. install a tiny launcher /app/bin/positron-app that execs the apphost,
  5. install the .desktop, .metainfo.xml, and icon into the standard /app/share tree.

finish-args grant exactly what a WebKitGTK app needs and nothing more:

Arg Why --socket=wayland Native Wayland display. --socket=fallback-x11 X11 fallback when Wayland is absent. --share=ipc WebKitGTK is multi-process; its processes need shared memory / IPC. --device=dri GPU access for accelerated compositing. --share=network Most web UIs load remote resources (drop it for a fully offline app). --filesystem=xdg-documents, --filesystem=xdg-download Minimal file access for open/save dialogs.

docs.title: Prerequisites (Linux host)
docs.text:
flatpak install flathub org.flatpak.Builder
flatpak install flathub org.gnome.Platform//49 org.gnome.Sdk//49

.NET 11 SDK on PATH (or set DOTNET).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
cd scripts/packaging
./flatpak-build.sh

Override the app for your own project:

APP_ID=com.example.MyApp \
APP_NAME=MyApp \
PROJECT=../../src/MyApp/MyApp.csproj \
./flatpak-build.sh

The script:

  1. publishes linux-x64 self-contained into flatpak/publish/,
  2. builds with flatpak run org.flatpak.Builder --force-clean --repo=repo builddir <manifest>,
  3. exports a bundle with flatpak build-bundle repo PositronApp.flatpak <app-id> --runtime-repo=https://dl.flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo.

--runtime-repo embeds where to fetch the GNOME runtime so a user installing the bundle pulls the dependency automatically:

flatpak install --user scripts/packaging/flatpak/PositronApp.flatpak
flatpak run io.github.positron.PositronApp

docs.title: Format tradeoffs: Flatpak vs AppImage vs .deb
docs.text:
• Flatpak (this script): sandboxed, runtime-shared (WebKitGTK comes from org.gnome.Platform, patched by the runtime vendor), distributable via Flathub. Best default for a cross-distro desktop app, and the only format where you get WebKitGTK for free from the runtime.
  • AppImage: a single portable file, no install, but no shared runtime — you must bundle WebKitGTK and its dependencies yourself, which is fragile across distros and inflates the file.
  • .deb/.rpm: native package managers, but per-distro packaging work and you depend on the distro shipping a compatible libwebkit2gtk-4.1 (most do, as libwebkit2gtk-4.1-0). Good when you target one distro family; poor for broad reach.

For broad, low-maintenance distribution with the WebKit dependency solved by the runtime, Flatpak is the recommended path.

docs.text:

  • Available runtimes (GNOME)
  • Single-file bundles
  • Flathub submission guide

docs.title: Packaging for macOS
docs.text:
Produces a universal (arm64 + x86_64) .app bundle, optionally code-signed, notarized, and stapled for distribution outside the Mac App Store.

Script: scripts/packaging/macos-bundle.sh Supporting files: Info.plist.template, entitlements.plist.

docs.title: Why it is hand-assembled
docs.text:
.NET has no first-party macOS .app bundler. dotnet publish gives you a bare apphost and its payload; turning that into a Finder-launchable, signable, notarizable bundle is manual work. The script automates the five steps Apple's tooling expects:

  1. Publish per-RID — dotnet publish -c Release -r osx-arm64 --self-contained and again for osx-x64. Self-contained means the .NET runtime is bundled; the end user needs no .NET install. WKWebView comes from the OS, so nothing WebView-related is bundled.
  2. lipo-merge the two apphosts into one universal binary (Apple: building a universal binary).
  3. Assemble PositronApp.app/Contents/{MacOS,Resources,Info.plist} by hand.
  4. Copy the publish payload (managed assemblies, native deps, your wwwroot) into Contents/MacOS next to the universal apphost.
  5. Sign → notarize → staple (only when SIGN_IDENTITY is set).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• macOS with Xcode command-line tools (lipo, codesign, xcrun, stapler).
  • .NET 11 SDK. If dotnet is not on PATH, set DOTNET=/path/to/dotnet.
  • For signing/notarizing only: an Apple Developer ID Application certificate in the keychain and a stored notarytool credential profile.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Unsigned bundle (fine for local use; Gatekeeper will quarantine it on other machines):

cd scripts/packaging
./macos-bundle.sh

Package your own app by overriding the variables at the top of the script:

APP_NAME=MyApp \
BUNDLE_ID=com.example.myapp \
VERSION=1.2.3 \
PROJECT=../../src/MyApp/MyApp.csproj \
./macos-bundle.sh

The finished bundle lands in artifacts/dist/<APP_NAME>.app. Confirm it:

plutil -lint artifacts/dist/MyApp.app/Contents/Info.plist
lipo -archs  artifacts/dist/MyApp.app/Contents/MacOS/MyApp   # -> x86_64 arm64
open artifacts/dist/MyApp.app

docs.title: Signing, notarizing, stapling
docs.text:
Signing is inside-out: nested Mach-O files (.dylib/.so) first, then the apphost (with entitlements), then the whole bundle last. The hardened runtime (--options runtime) is required for notarization. The script does all of this when you provide credentials:

# One-time: store notary credentials in the keychain.
xcrun notarytool store-credentials "positron-notary" \
  --apple-id you@example.com --team-id TEAMID --password <app-specific-password>

SIGN_IDENTITY="Developer ID Application: Your Name (TEAMID)" \
NOTARY_PROFILE="positron-notary" \
./macos-bundle.sh
  • SIGN_IDENTITY set, NOTARY_PROFILE unset → signed but not notarized.
  • Both unset → unsigned (the default; an echoed note explains the skip).

See Apple's Notarizing macOS software before distribution and Customizing the notarization workflow.

docs.title: Entitlements and NativeAOT
docs.text:
entitlements.plist is deliberately minimal. Positron publishes with NativeAOT by default (POSITRON_AOT=1): no JIT, no runtime code generation. That lets the file omit the JIT-oriented entitlements that a CLR normally needs:

  • com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit — omitted (NativeAOT never JITs).
  • com.apple.security.cs.allow-unsigned-executable-memory — omitted (JIT-only).
  • com.apple.security.cs.allow-dyld-environment-variables — omitted (not needed).
  • com.apple.security.cs.disable-library-validation — omitted; Positron only dlopens Apple-signed system frameworks, so library validation stays on.

If you set POSITRON_AOT=0 to publish a plain self-contained (JIT CoreCLR) build, you must add com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit to entitlements.plist or the app will fail the hardened runtime at launch. The comments in entitlements.plist spell out exactly which entitlement to add for which symptom.

docs.title: Info.plist
docs.text: Info.plist.template carries placeholders (__APP_NAME__, __BUNDLE_ID__, __VERSION__) that the script substitutes with sed. It sets CFBundlePackageType=APPL, NSHighResolutionCapable (Retina), and LSMinimumSystemVersion=11.0 (the Big Sur baseline matching the publish RIDs).

docs.title: Distribution format tradeoffs
docs.text: For most open-source Positron apps a signed + notarized .app inside a .dmg or .zip is the right default — it is the lowest-friction path and requires no first-party installer tooling. A .pkg installer is worth it only when you need pre/post-install scripts or to place files outside the app bundle. The Mac App Store imposes additional sandboxing and review and is out of scope for this script.

docs.title: Packaging for Windows
docs.text:
Produces a self-contained publish folder and a distributable .zip.

Script: scripts/packaging/windows-publish.ps1

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
1. dotnet publish -r win-x64 -c Release --self-contained — a folder of files with the .NET runtime bundled (no .NET install needed on the target machine).
  2. Verifies WebView2Loader.dll is present in the output.
  3. Zips the folder into artifacts/dist/<AppName>-<Version>-win-x64.zip.

A commented single-file variant and a commented signtool section are included for when you need them.

docs.title: WebView2: Evergreen vs Fixed Version
docs.text:
Positron renders through WebView2 (Edge/Chromium). Two runtime distribution modes:

  • Evergreen Runtime (recommended default): installed and auto-updated by the OS. It is preinstalled on Windows 11; on older Windows it may be missing. Your app should detect it at runtime and, if absent, run the ~2 MB bootstrapper (MicrosoftEdgeWebview2Setup.exe). The canonical detection call is CoreWebView2Environment.GetAvailableBrowserVersionString() — a null/throw means "not installed". Download the bootstrapper from the WebView2 page.
  • Fixed Version Runtime: a versioned runtime folder you redistribute with the app and point WebView2 at explicitly. Larger (~150 MB) but removes the install/update dependency — the right choice for offline or locked-down deployments.

Either way, the native loader shim WebView2Loader.dll must ship next to the executable — it is what Positron's P/Invoke binds to in order to find and start the runtime. The script warns if it is missing from the publish output; it is normally supplied by the Microsoft.Web.WebView2 package (copy it from the SDK's runtimes/win-x64/native folder if not). See WebView2 distribution.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Windows with PowerShell 5.1+ (or PowerShell 7).
  • .NET 11 SDK (dotnet on PATH, or installed at %ProgramFiles%\dotnet).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
cd scripts\packaging
./windows-publish.ps1

Override for your own app:

./windows-publish.ps1 -AppName MyApp -Version 1.2.3 `
  -Project ..\..\src\MyApp\MyApp.csproj

Variables can also come from the environment (APP_NAME, PROJECT, VERSION, PUBLISH_DIR, DIST_DIR), matching the other platform scripts.

docs.title: Single-file variant
docs.text:
The script's default is a multi-file folder publish — simplest to sign and it keeps WebView2Loader.dll visible as a sibling. A single-file publish is available (commented):

dotnet publish ... -p:PublishSingleFile=true -p:IncludeNativeLibrariesForSelfExtract=true

IncludeNativeLibrariesForSelfExtract=true is mandatory for single-file here: native libraries such as WebView2Loader.dll cannot be loaded from inside the bundle, so they must extract to disk at startup, or WebView2 fails to initialize. See single-file deployment.

docs.title: Code signing
docs.text:
Authenticode signing is commented in the script. Two facts that trip people up:

  • SHA-256 is mandatory. signtool now requires /fd SHA256 (file digest) and /td SHA256 (timestamp digest); SHA-1 is rejected. Always include a timestamp server (/tr) so the signature survives certificate expiry.
  • Keys must live in hardware. As of 2023+, CA/Browser Forum rules require OV and EV code-signing private keys to live on an HSM / hardware token or a cloud signing service (e.g. Azure Trusted Signing via signtool's /dlib provider). A plain .pfx on disk only works for self-signed / internal certificates.
# Hardware-token / cert-store certificate:
signtool sign /fd SHA256 /tr http://timestamp.digicert.com /td SHA256 `
  /n "Your Company, Inc." "$PublishDir\MyApp.exe"

Re-zip after signing so the distributed archive contains the signed binary. See signtool.

docs.title: Format tradeoffs: folder/zip vs MSIX vs Velopack
docs.text:
• Folder + .zip (this script): zero extra tooling, trivial to sign, works everywhere. No install/uninstall integration or auto-update. Best default for a simple distribution.
  • MSIX: modern Windows installer with clean install/uninstall and Store eligibility, but it requires signing even for sideloading and adds packaging complexity. Choose it when you need Store distribution or managed enterprise deployment.
  • Velopack / Squirrel: third-party frameworks that add delta auto-updates and a friendly installer on top of a publish folder. Choose when in-app auto-update is a priority and you do not want MSIX.

docs.text:

  • WebView2 distribution
  • signtool

docs.title: Tutorial: an Angular app
docs.text:
Angular (and any SPA) runs in Positron by serving its production build over app://localhost/. The app:// origin is what makes this work: absolute /asset paths resolve, and unknown routes fall back to index.html, so the Angular router behaves exactly as it does on the web.

The runnable source is in samples/angular (the Angular app) and samples/angular-host (the Positron host).

cd samples/angular && npm install && npx ng build   # build the SPA
dotnet run --project samples/angular-host            # serve + run it

docs.title: 1. Create the Angular app
docs.text:
Scaffold with the Angular CLI as usual:

npx @angular/cli@20 new positron-ng --routing --style css --ssr false

Angular CLI and Node version

The latest Angular CLI (v21+) requires Node ^22.22.3 || ^24.15.0 || >=26. On an older Node 24 (e.g. 24.13), pin @angular/cli@20 as shown. Upgrade Node to use the newest CLI.

Leave the default <base href="/"> in index.html — it is correct for the app://localhost/ origin. (Do not switch to a relative base; that's only for file://, which Positron does not use.)

docs.title: 2. Declare and call the bridge
docs.text:
Add a type declaration so TypeScript knows about window.positron (src/positron.d.ts):

interface PositronApi {
  invoke<T = unknown>(channel: string, payload?: unknown): Promise<T>;
  on(channel: string, cb: (payload: unknown) => void): () => void;
}
declare global {
  interface Window { positron: PositronApi; }
}
export {};

Wrap IPC in a service (src/app/positron.service.ts):

import { Injectable } from "@angular/core";

@Injectable({ providedIn: "root" })
export class PositronService {
  greet(name: string): Promise<{ message: string }> {
    return window.positron.invoke("greet", { name });
  }
}

Use it from a component as you would any service. The build output lands in dist/positron-ng/browser (the @angular/build:application builder nests it under browser/).

docs.title: 3. The Positron host
docs.text:
A tiny C# host points ServeDirectory at the Angular build and registers the greet channel:

using System.Text.Json.Serialization;
using Positron;

// dist/positron-ng/browser relative to this host project.
string distDir = Path.GetFullPath(Path.Combine(
    AppContext.BaseDirectory, "..", "..", "..", "..", "angular", "dist", "positron-ng", "browser"));

var options = new WindowOptions
{
    Title = "Positron — Angular",
    ServeDirectory = distDir,
};

App.Run(options, window =>
{
    window.Handle<GreetRequest, GreetResponse>("greet", req =>
        new GreetResponse($"Hello, {req.Name}! — greeted by C#"));
    window.LoadUrl("app://localhost/");
}, AngularHostJsonContext.Default.Options);

internal sealed record GreetRequest(string Name);
internal sealed record GreetResponse(string Message);

[JsonSourceGenerationOptions(PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonKnownNamingPolicy.CamelCase)]
[JsonSerializable(typeof(GreetRequest))]
[JsonSerializable(typeof(GreetResponse))]
internal sealed partial class AngularHostJsonContext : JsonSerializerContext { }

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Serve dist/<project>/browser, not dist/<project>. The modern Angular builder adds the browser/ subfolder. If you rename the project from positron-ng, update the host path.
  • Rebuild after web changes. ng build must run before the host serves updated files. For a fast inner loop during development you can run ng serve and point window.LoadUrl at http://localhost:4200/ instead, then switch back to app:// serving for the shipped app.
  • Routing just works because app:// falls back to index.html for client-side routes.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• React — the same pattern with Vite.
  • Packaging — bundle the Angular host + its dist for distribution.

docs.title: Tutorial: context menus
docs.text:
By default a Positron window shows the WebView's built-in context menu (the OS/engine default). You control it with two WindowOptions:

  • ContextMenu — ContextMenuMode.Default (show it) or ContextMenuMode.Disabled (suppress it).
  • EnableDevTools — true to allow the WebView's developer tools (right-click → Inspect, where the platform supports it). Leave false in release builds.
var options = new WindowOptions
{
    Title = "My App",
    ContextMenu = ContextMenuMode.Disabled, // no default right-click menu
    EnableDevTools = true,                  // dev tools during development
};

docs.title: Providing your own menu
docs.text:
A custom context menu is ordinary web UI: disable the default menu in the host, then handle the contextmenu event in the page. This is exactly what the text editor does — a one-item menu with a "Save" action:

const menu = document.getElementById("menu"); // a styled, hidden <div> of buttons

document.addEventListener("contextmenu", (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();                 // stop the (already-disabled) default
  menu.style.left = e.clientX + "px";
  menu.style.top = e.clientY + "px";
  menu.style.display = "block";
});

// Dismiss on any left click or Escape.
document.addEventListener("click", () => { menu.style.display = "none"; });
document.addEventListener("keydown", (e) => { if (e.key === "Escape") menu.style.display = "none"; });

document.getElementById("menu-save").addEventListener("click", () => {
  menu.style.display = "none";
  save(); // your action — may call window.positron.invoke(...) to reach C#
});

<div id="menu">
  <button id="menu-save">Save</button>
  <!-- add more items here -->
</div>

Because the menu is HTML, you style it with CSS (the sample uses the Canvas/CanvasText/ Highlight system colors so it matches light and dark mode automatically) and its actions are just JavaScript — including window.positron.invoke(...) calls into your C# handlers.

Why an in-page menu rather than a native one?

An HTML menu is consistent across macOS/Windows/Linux, styleable, and needs no extra API. For a native application menu bar, that's a separate (future) capability; for right-click menus, the in-page approach is the simplest thing that works everywhere.

docs.title: Developer tools
docs.text: During development, set EnableDevTools = true and right-click → Inspect (macOS/Windows). This is the WebView's real inspector — DOM, console, network, and sources — so you debug the renderer exactly as you would a web page. Turn it off for release builds.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Text editor — the custom menu in a complete app.
  • Security — why disabling the default menu is common for app-like UIs.

docs.title: Tutorial: the file system
docs.text:
Positron mediates all filesystem access through the C# host — the web page never gets raw disk access. You reach the filesystem two ways:

  1. Built-in bridges for the common cases — native open/save dialogs and UTF‑8 text I/O — callable straight from JavaScript with no host code.
  2. Your own handlers (window.Handle) when you need something the built-ins don't cover (binary files, directories, app-specific validation, etc.).

docs.title: Built-in dialogs and text I/O (from JavaScript)
docs.text:
These are injected on window.positron automatically; the host registers nothing.

// Open: resolves to an absolute path, or null if the user cancels.
const path = await window.positron.dialog.open({
  title: "Open a document",            // optional
  allowedExtensions: ["txt", "md"],    // optional, no leading dot
  initialDirectory: "/Users/me/Docs",  // optional
});

// Save: resolves to the chosen path, or null if cancelled.
const target = await window.positron.dialog.save({
  suggestedFileName: "untitled.txt",
  allowedExtensions: ["txt"],
});

// Text I/O by absolute path (UTF-8).
const text = await window.positron.fs.readText(path);
await window.positron.fs.writeText(target, "new contents");

The text editor tutorial is a complete app built from exactly these calls.

docs.title: The same dialogs from C
docs.text:
If you'd rather drive the dialog from the host (e.g. in response to a menu or a timer), Window exposes them directly:

App.Run(options, async window =>  // configure may be async
{
    string? path = await window.ShowOpenFileAsync(new Positron.Files.OpenFileOptions
    {
        AllowedExtensions = new[] { "txt", "md" },
    });

    if (path is not null)
    {
        string text = await File.ReadAllTextAsync(path);
        // ... use it, or push it to the page with window.Emit(...)
    }
}, MyJsonContext.Default.Options);

OpenFileOptions and SaveFileOptions (namespace Positron.Files) carry Title, AllowedExtensions, InitialDirectory, and — for save — SuggestedFileName. See the File Dialogs API.

docs.title: Writing your own file handler
docs.text:
When the built-ins aren't enough, register a handler and call it with window.positron.invoke. Here's a "read any file as base64" operation, which the built-in text API doesn't provide:

// C# host
window.Handle<ReadRequest, string>("readBinaryBase64", async req =>
{
    byte[] bytes = await File.ReadAllBytesAsync(req.Path);
    return Convert.ToBase64String(bytes);
});

internal sealed record ReadRequest(string Path);

// renderer
const b64 = await window.positron.invoke("readBinaryBase64", { path });

Remember to add ReadRequest (and any result types) to your [JsonSerializable] context.

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
• Validate paths at the boundary. A handler receives whatever the renderer sends. If an argument is a path, treat it as untrusted: constrain it to an expected root, reject traversal, etc. See Security.
  • The page can't read files on its own. There is no fs in the renderer beyond the narrow, host-implemented window.positron.fs surface — exactly the point of the contextBridge-style model.
  • Handler exceptions don't leak. If your handler throws (e.g. FileNotFoundException), the renderer gets a generic rejection; the real exception is surfaced host-side for logging, not sent to the page.

docs.title: Tutorial: a React app
docs.text:
React runs in Positron the same way every SPA does: build it, serve the output over app://localhost/. This tutorial uses Vite (the current React default); Create React App or any other bundler works identically — you just serve its dist/build folder.

The runnable source is in samples/react (the Vite app) and samples/react-host (the Positron host).

cd samples/react && npm install && npm run build   # build the SPA → dist/
dotnet run --project samples/react-host             # serve + run it

docs.title: 1. Create the React app
docs.text:
npm create vite@latest positron-react -- --template react-ts

In vite.config.ts, keep (or set) base: "/" — the built index.html then references /assets/..., which resolve against the app://localhost/ origin:

import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react()],
  base: "/", // correct for app://; do NOT use "./" (that's for file:// origins)
});

docs.title: 2. Declare and call the bridge
docs.text:
Type declaration (src/positron.d.ts):

interface PositronApi {
  invoke<T = unknown>(channel: string, payload?: unknown): Promise<T>;
  on(channel: string, cb: (payload: unknown) => void): () => void;
}
declare global {
  interface Window { positron: PositronApi; }
}
export {};

A small service (src/positronService.ts):

export function greet(name: string): Promise<{ message: string }> {
  return window.positron.invoke("greet", { name });
}

Use it from a component:

import { useState } from "react";
import { greet } from "./positronService";

export default function App() {
  const [name, setName] = useState("world");
  const [msg, setMsg] = useState("");
  return (
    <>
      <input value={name} onChange={(e) => setName(e.target.value)} />
      <button onClick={async () => setMsg((await greet(name)).message)}>Greet via C#</button>
      <p>{msg}</p>
    </>
  );
}

docs.title: 3. The Positron host
docs.text:
Point ServeDirectory at Vite's dist and register the channel:

using System.Text.Json.Serialization;
using Positron;

// samples/react/dist relative to this host project.
string distDir = Path.GetFullPath(Path.Combine(
    AppContext.BaseDirectory, "..", "..", "..", "..", "react", "dist"));

var options = new WindowOptions
{
    Title = "Positron — React",
    ServeDirectory = distDir,
};

App.Run(options, window =>
{
    window.Handle<GreetRequest, GreetResponse>("greet", req =>
        new GreetResponse($"Hello, {req.Name}! — greeted by C#"));
    window.LoadUrl("app://localhost/");
}, ReactHostJsonContext.Default.Options);

internal sealed record GreetRequest(string Name);
internal sealed record GreetResponse(string Message);

[JsonSourceGenerationOptions(PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonKnownNamingPolicy.CamelCase)]
[JsonSerializable(typeof(GreetRequest))]
[JsonSerializable(typeof(GreetResponse))]
internal sealed partial class ReactHostJsonContext : JsonSerializerContext { }

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• base: "/", not "./". Positron serves over a real origin (app://localhost/), so absolute asset paths are correct. Relative bases are a file:// workaround Positron doesn't need.
  • Rebuild after web changes, or use Vite's dev server (npm run dev) and point window.LoadUrl at http://localhost:5173/ during development, switching to app:// for the shipped build.
  • Client-side routing works — app:// falls back to index.html for unknown routes, so React Router (or any history-API router) behaves normally.

docs.title: Tutorial: a text editor
docs.text:
This is the canonical first "real" Positron app: a tiny text editor that opens a file from disk, lets you edit it in the web UI, and saves it back. It ties together the three things most desktop apps need — serving a web UI, native file dialogs, and file I/O — in about 40 lines of C# and 60 lines of HTML/JS.

The complete, runnable source is in samples/Positron.Sample.TextEditor.

dotnet run --project samples/Positron.Sample.TextEditor

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The app uses only the built-in bridges Positron injects into the page, so the C# host registers no channels of its own:

  • window.positron.dialog.open(options) / .save(options) — native open/save dialogs, resolving to an absolute path or null if cancelled.
  • window.positron.fs.readText(path) / .writeText(path, contents) — UTF‑8 text file I/O, mediated by the C# host (the web page never gets raw filesystem access).

The UI is a static wwwroot folder served over app://localhost/ — the recommended way to ship a web UI (real origin, absolute /asset paths, history-API fallback). See Serving a web UI for why.

docs.title: The C# host
docs.text:
Program.cs is almost entirely configuration — serve the folder, disable the default context menu (the page supplies its own), and load the app:

using System.Text.Json.Serialization;
using Positron;

var options = new WindowOptions
{
    Title = "Positron — Text Editor",
    Width = 760,
    Height = 560,
    ServeDirectory = AppContext.BaseDirectory + "wwwroot", // ServeEntry defaults to index.html
    ContextMenu = ContextMenuMode.Disabled,                // page provides its own menu
};

App.Run(options, window =>
{
    window.LoadUrl("app://localhost/");
}, TextEditorJsonContext.Default.Options);

return 0;

// App.Run requires a source-generated JSON context (for trim/AOT safety). This app calls only the
// built-in channels, so it has no payload types of its own — but the generator needs at least one
// [JsonSerializable] to emit the context, so we register the primitive the built-ins use.
[JsonSourceGenerationOptions(PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonKnownNamingPolicy.CamelCase)]
[JsonSerializable(typeof(string))]
internal sealed partial class TextEditorJsonContext : JsonSerializerContext { }

Why a JSON context with no app types?

App.Run requires a JsonSerializerContext so your app stays trim- and NativeAOT-safe. An empty source-gen context won't compile (the generator emits nothing), so add at least one [JsonSerializable(typeof(string))]. The library's own built-in payloads are registered internally.

docs.title: The web UI
docs.text:
wwwroot/index.html is a header with Open/Save buttons, a <textarea>, and a one-item custom context menu:

<header>
  <button id="open">Open</button>
  <button id="save">Save</button>
  <span id="path">(no file)</span>
</header>
<textarea id="editor" spellcheck="false" placeholder="Open a .txt or .md file…"></textarea>
<div id="menu"><button id="menu-save">Save</button></div>
<script src="/app.js"></script>

wwwroot/app.js is the whole behavior — open, save, and the context menu:

let currentPath = null; // absolute path of the current file, or null for an unsaved buffer

async function open() {
  const path = await window.positron.dialog.open({ allowedExtensions: ["txt", "md"] });
  if (!path) return;                                  // user cancelled
  editor.value = await window.positron.fs.readText(path);
  setPath(path);
}

async function save() {
  let path = currentPath;
  if (!path) {                                        // first save → ask where
    path = await window.positron.dialog.save({
      allowedExtensions: ["txt", "md"],
      suggestedFileName: "untitled.txt",
    });
    if (!path) return;                                // user cancelled
  }
  await window.positron.fs.writeText(path, editor.value);
  setPath(path);
}

document.getElementById("open").addEventListener("click", open);
document.getElementById("save").addEventListener("click", save);

The custom right-click menu — shown because the host set ContextMenu = Disabled — is a plain DOM element toggled on the contextmenu event:

const menu = document.getElementById("menu");
document.addEventListener("contextmenu", (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  menu.style.left = e.clientX + "px";
  menu.style.top = e.clientY + "px";
  menu.style.display = "block";
});
document.addEventListener("click", () => { menu.style.display = "none"; });
document.getElementById("menu-save").addEventListener("click", () => { menu.style.display = "none"; save(); });

docs.title: What to take away
docs.text:
• File access lives in C#. The dialogs and file I/O run in the host; the renderer only ever sees a path string and file contents it explicitly asked for. This is the same trust boundary Electron gets from contextBridge.
  • The UI is just the web. Everything except the four window.positron.* calls is ordinary HTML/JS you could paste into any browser.
  • No channels to wire for common file operations — the built-ins cover open/save/read/write. When you need app-specific operations, register your own with window.Handle(...); see the file-system tutorial and IPC.

docs.text:

  • Context menus — the default menu, disabling it, dev tools, and custom menus.
  • Packaging — ship this editor as a macOS .app, a Linux Flatpak, or a Windows folder.

docs.title: Tutorial: custom web components
docs.text:
Positron has no opinion about your frontend — any web technology works, including the platform's own component model, custom elements. This tutorial builds a reusable <positron-greeter> element that talks to C#.

The runnable source is in samples/web-components.

dotnet run --project samples/web-components

docs.title: The element
docs.text:
A standard custom element with Shadow DOM. The only Positron-specific line is the window.positron.invoke call — everything else is vanilla Web Components:

class PositronGreeter extends HTMLElement {
  constructor() {
    super();
    this.attachShadow({ mode: "open" });
  }

  connectedCallback() {
    const name = this.getAttribute("name") || "world";
    this.shadowRoot.innerHTML = `
      <input value="${name}" aria-label="name" />
      <button>Greet via C#</button>
      <output>Result will appear here.</output>
    `;

    const input = this.shadowRoot.querySelector("input");
    const output = this.shadowRoot.querySelector("output");
    this.shadowRoot.querySelector("button").addEventListener("click", async () => {
      try {
        const res = await window.positron.invoke("greet", { name: input.value });
        output.textContent = res.message;
      } catch (e) {
        output.textContent = "error: " + e.message;
      }
    });
  }
}

customElements.define("positron-greeter", PositronGreeter);

Use it anywhere in your markup:

<positron-greeter name="world"></positron-greeter>

window.positron is available inside Shadow DOM

window.positron is a global installed by the preload bridge, so it's reachable from inside a custom element's shadow root just like any other window API. No special wiring needed.

docs.title: The host
docs.text:
Serve the folder over app:// and register the one channel the element invokes:

var options = new WindowOptions
{
    Title = "Positron — Web Components",
    ServeDirectory = AppContext.BaseDirectory + "wwwroot",
};

App.Run(options, window =>
{
    window.Handle<GreetRequest, GreetResponse>("greet", req =>
        new GreetResponse($"Hello, {req.Name}! — greeted by C#"));

    window.LoadUrl("app://localhost/");
}, WebComponentsJsonContext.Default.Options);

internal sealed record GreetRequest(string Name);
internal sealed record GreetResponse(string Message);

[JsonSourceGenerationOptions(PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonKnownNamingPolicy.CamelCase)]
[JsonSerializable(typeof(GreetRequest))]
[JsonSerializable(typeof(GreetResponse))]
internal sealed partial class WebComponentsJsonContext : JsonSerializerContext { }

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Custom elements need no build step or framework, but if you want to use a component library (Lit, Shoelace, FAST, etc.), install it with npm and either bundle it or load it from your served wwwroot. Because the app runs over the app:// origin, absolute module paths and import work the same as on the web — put the dependency's files under ServeDirectory and reference them with an absolute path (/vendor/lit.js) or an import map. For a full framework build pipeline, see the Angular and React tutorials, which follow the same serve-the-dist-folder pattern.

docs.text:

  • IPC — the invoke/Handle contract.

docs.title: Tutorial: a plain web UI
docs.text: The simplest Positron app is a C# host plus a folder of static web files. There are two ways to get your HTML into the window; this tutorial covers both and explains when to use each.

docs.title: Option A — serve a folder over app:// (recommended)
docs.text:
Point WindowOptions.ServeDirectory at a folder and load app://localhost/. The folder is served with a real web origin: absolute /asset paths work, fetch/import work, and unknown routes fall back to index.html (so client-side routing works). This is the right choice for anything beyond a single inline page, and the only correct choice for SPA frameworks (Angular, React).

using System.Text.Json.Serialization;
using Positron;

var options = new WindowOptions
{
    Title = "My App",
    Width = 900,
    Height = 600,
    ServeDirectory = AppContext.BaseDirectory + "wwwroot", // ServeEntry defaults to index.html
};

App.Run(options, window =>
{
    window.Handle<GreetRequest, GreetResponse>("greet", req => new GreetResponse($"Hello, {req.Name}!"));
    window.LoadUrl("app://localhost/");
}, AppJsonContext.Default.Options);

return 0;

internal sealed record GreetRequest(string Name);
internal sealed record GreetResponse(string Message);

[JsonSourceGenerationOptions(PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonKnownNamingPolicy.CamelCase)]
[JsonSerializable(typeof(GreetRequest))]
[JsonSerializable(typeof(GreetResponse))]
internal sealed partial class AppJsonContext : JsonSerializerContext { }

Copy the folder next to the executable in your .csproj:

<ItemGroup>
  <Content Include="wwwroot\**" CopyToOutputDirectory="PreserveNewest" />
</ItemGroup>

wwwroot/index.html:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8" />
  <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"
        content="default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'self';" />
  <title>My App</title>
</head>
<body>
  <input id="name" value="world" />
  <button id="greet">Greet</button>
  <div id="out"></div>
  <script src="/app.js"></script>
</body>
</html>

wwwroot/app.js:

document.getElementById("greet").addEventListener("click", async () => {
  const name = document.getElementById("name").value;
  const res = await window.positron.invoke("greet", { name });
  document.getElementById("out").textContent = res.message;
});

docs.title: Option B — inline HTML with LoadHtml
docs.text:
For a one-file demo or a splash screen, pass HTML directly — no folder, no serving:

App.Run(options, window =>
{
    window.Handle<GreetRequest, GreetResponse>("greet", req => new GreetResponse($"Hello, {req.Name}!"));
    window.LoadHtml("<!doctype html><button onclick=\"…\">Greet</button>…");
}, AppJsonContext.Default.Options);

LoadHtml is handy for tiny UIs (the bundled Positron.Sample.Hello uses it), but there's no origin and no asset resolution — external src/href and absolute paths won't resolve. Use Option A for anything real.

docs.title: Talking to C
docs.text:
Both options expose the same bridge:

  • window.positron.invoke(channel, payload) → a Promise resolved by your C# Handle handler.
  • window.positron.on(channel, cb) → subscribe to events the host pushes with window.Emit(...); returns an unsubscribe function.

See IPC for the full contract, and the file system for the built-in dialog/file bridges.
